Colorado's primary draw is how you get into the best elk units and seasons. It is not hard once you understand the pieces, but missing one step, like buying your qualifying license, can knock you out of the draw for the year. Here is how it works.

Key dates

These are CPW's dates for the 2026 draw. The 2027 dates will be in next year's Big Game brochure, but the calendar has followed the same pattern for years.

Step 1: Get your hunter education card

Anyone born on or after January 1, 1949, must have completed hunter education before applying. Colorado accepts hunter education cards from other states. You will also need a valid ID and, if you are 12 or older, a Social Security number or ITIN.

Step 2: Buy a qualifying license

You cannot apply for the draw until you own a current-year qualifying license. You can buy it in the same online checkout as your application, but it has to go in your cart first.

The cheapest qualifying license for most people is the annual small game license:

The small game license is useful in its own right. It covers small game like grouse and rabbits, so bring a shotgun on your elk trip.

Step 3: Choose up to four hunt codes

Every elk hunt in Colorado has a hunt code that sets the unit, season, sex, and weapon. For example, a code tells you whether a license is for a bull, a cow, or either sex, and whether it is for archery, muzzleloader, or a specific rifle season.

You can list up to four choices on one elk application. You can draw only one elk license in the primary draw.

How to think about your four choices:

  • 1st choice: The hunt you really want. This is the only choice that uses your preference points.
  • 2nd to 4th choices: Hunts with leftover licenses in past years, or cow tags, so you still get to hunt if your first choice does not come through.
  • Points only: If you want to build points for a future hunt, you can apply for a preference point only and not hunt this year.

CPW publishes draw statistics showing how many points it took to draw each hunt code in past years. Check them before you choose.

Step 4: Understand preference points

If you do not draw your first choice, you earn a preference point for elk. Points only come from the primary draw. When you do draw your first choice, your points reset to zero.

Some hunt codes can be drawn with zero points. Premium units can take 20 or more years. Most hunters build points for a few years while hunting OTC or leftover tags in the meantime.

Nonresident quotas: Nonresidents compete for a share of the licenses. For hunt codes that took six or more points for residents to draw, up to 20% can go to nonresidents. For elk hunts that took fewer than six points, up to 25% can go to nonresidents.

Step 5: Apply alone or as a group

Elk group applications can have any number of hunters. Everyone in the group must list the same hunt choices, and the group draws together or not at all. Groups do not improve your odds.

Be careful with groups. If one member makes an error on their application, the whole group is disqualified. Groups that mix residents and nonresidents will not get licenses if the nonresident cap for that hunt has already been reached.

Step 6: Pay and confirm

Application fees ($11.49 per species for nonresidents and $8.93 for residents in 2026) are not refundable. You pay for the elk license itself only if you draw. Check your results in your CPW account in late May. If you drew a license you can no longer use, you can surrender it by the deadline and get your points back.

What it costs to apply (nonresident example, 2026)

Point rules at a glance

  • System: Preference points. First-choice licenses go to the applicants with the most points. Hunt codes that took 10 or more resident points the year before also run a small random hybrid draw for applicants with 5 or more points.
  • Nonresident share: Up to 20% of licenses in hunt codes that took 6 or more points, and up to 25% in codes that took fewer. The caps don't apply to the secondary draw or leftovers.
  • You lose your points if: you draw your first choice (hybrid licenses included), or go 10 straight years without applying for or holding a elk license.
  • Waiting period: None.
  • Groups: No size limit, but the whole group draws at the point level of the member with the fewest points. Hybrid codes don't allow groups.
  • Point only: List hunt code P-999-99-P as your first choice. There's no point fee for elk in 2026, but you still need the qualifying license and application fee.

Didn't draw? You still have options

  • Secondary draw (June): Licenses left over from the primary draw. It does not use your preference points, and nonresident caps do not apply.
  • Leftover licenses (August): Anything left after the secondary draw goes on sale first-come, first-served.
  • Over-the-counter tags: Residents can buy OTC tags in many units, and nonresidents still have some OTC options. See what is still available.
  • Landowner vouchers: Some outfitters offer hunts on private land with landowner preference vouchers. These are not sold by CPW and can be transferred only once, from the landowner to the hunter.

Many Colorado outfitters will tell you which hunt codes they guide and what your draw odds look like, and some help clients apply. If you're booking a guided hunt, call them before the April deadline.

Because almost every Colorado deer license is limited, the primary draw is where your deer season is decided. A good application is mostly about choosing the right hunt codes for your points and not missing a step. Here is how it works.

Key dates

These are CPW's dates for the 2026 draw. The 2027 dates will be in next year's Big Game brochure, but the calendar has followed the same pattern for years.

Step 1: Hunter education and ID

Anyone born on or after January 1, 1949, needs a hunter education card before applying. Colorado accepts cards from other states. Applicants 12 and older also need a Social Security number or ITIN.

Step 2: Buy a qualifying license

Every applicant, including youth, must own a current-year qualifying license before applying. You can buy it in the same checkout as your application.

The Habitat Stamp ($12.76 for ages 18 to 64) is added to your first purchase.

Step 3: Read the deer hunt codes

Each deer hunt has a hunt code that sets the sex, unit, season, and weapon. The second letter tells you the sex: M is antlered (buck), F is antlerless (doe), and E is either sex. The last letter is the weapon: A for archery, M for muzzleloader, R for rifle. For example, an early high-country rifle buck hunt in the Flat Tops is coded DM012E1R.

Check the brochure for restrictions such as whitetail only, private land only, or youth only.

Step 4: Choose up to four hunts

You can list up to four choices on one deer application, and you can draw only one deer license in the primary draw.

  • 1st choice: The hunt you want most. It is the only choice that uses or earns preference points.
  • 2nd to 4th choices: Hunts that had licenses left over in past years, doe hunts, or plains hunts. These are your backup plan.
  • Point only: If you don't want to hunt this year, list the preference point code (P-999-99-P) as your first choice.

Check CPW's draw statistics to see how many points each code took in past years. Deer points are free in 2026 beyond the application fee.

Step 5: Understand preference points

You earn one deer preference point each year you miss your first choice or apply for a point only. Your points reset to zero when you draw your first choice. Points expire if you go 10 straight years without applying for or holding a deer license.

What to expect: Draw odds vary enormously. Many doe, plains, and whitetail hunt codes have historically drawn with few or no points. Popular mountain buck units and late rifle seasons take more, and the most sought-after trophy units take well over a decade. As one example, buck licenses in GMU 512 took 11 resident points and 12 nonresident points in the 2024 draw. Point creep is real, so the points a hunt took last year may not be enough this year.

Step 6: The hybrid draw

For the highest-demand deer hunts, CPW sets aside some licenses for a random hybrid draw. A hunt code qualifies if it took 10 or more resident points to draw the year before and has at least five licenses. You must have at least five deer points, apply on your own (no groups), and list the hybrid code as your first choice. If you win, you lose all your deer points. If you miss, you earn a point.

Step 7: Know the nonresident quotas

Nonresidents compete for a share of each hunt code:

  • Hunt codes that took six or more resident points: up to 20% of licenses can go to nonresidents.
  • Hunt codes that took fewer than six points: up to 25% can go to nonresidents.

These caps do not apply in the secondary draw or to leftover licenses.

Step 8: Apply alone or as a group

Deer group applications can include any number of hunters. Everyone lists the same hunt codes in the same order, and the group draws at the point level of its lowest member. Youth lose their youth preference in a group, and one member's error can disqualify everyone.

Step 9: Results and payment

The application fee ($8.93 for residents and $11.49 for nonresidents in 2026) is not refundable. You pay for the license only if you draw. If you draw a license you can't use, surrender it by the deadline. CPW refunds the license fee and restores your points.

What it costs to apply (nonresident example, 2026)

Changes coming in 2028

CPW has approved a new draw system that starts with the 2028 draw. Each hunt code will be split between a preference point draw and a bonus draw, nonresidents will get a flat 25% share, the point-only hunt code goes away, and a preference point fee is planned. Existing points carry over, but their value may change.

Point rules at a glance

  • System: Preference points. First-choice licenses go to the applicants with the most points. Hunt codes that took 10 or more resident points the year before also run a small random hybrid draw for applicants with 5 or more points.
  • Nonresident share: Up to 20% of licenses in hunt codes that took 6 or more points, and up to 25% in codes that took fewer. The caps don't apply to the secondary draw or leftovers.
  • You lose your points if: you draw your first choice (hybrid licenses included), or go 10 straight years without applying for or holding a deer license.
  • Waiting period: None.
  • Groups: No size limit, but the whole group draws at the point level of the member with the fewest points. Hybrid codes don't allow groups.
  • Point only: List hunt code P-999-99-P as your first choice. There's no point fee for deer in 2026, but you still need the qualifying license and application fee.

California's Big Game Drawing is the only way to get a premium deer tag, like an X zone mule deer hunt or a C zone tag. It is also how many hunters lock in an A, B, or D zone tag early. The system is simpler than most western draws, but a few rules can cost you a year of points if you miss them.

Key dates

These are CDFW's dates for the 2026 drawing. The 2027 dates will be in next year's Big Game Hunting Digest, but the calendar has followed the same pattern for years.

Step 1: Get a hunting license and hunter education on file

You need a current annual California hunting license to apply. The 2026–27 license costs $64.54 for residents and $225.46 for nonresidents. The two-day nonresident license is not valid for deer.

If you have never bought a California license before, you need proof of hunter education: a California certificate, a hunter education certificate from another state or province, or a valid hunting license from a prior year or another state. Hunter education has to be on file before you can buy online.

Step 2: Buy your first deer tag application

In California, your deer application and your deer tag are the same purchase. The first deer tag application costs $42.38 for residents and $377.35 for nonresidents. If you draw, that is your tag. If you don't, you can use the application to buy an unrestricted tag later.

Hunters must be at least 12 by July 1 to apply. Second deer tag applications in the drawing are only for junior hunters applying for apprentice hunts.

Step 3: Choose up to three hunts

You can list up to three deer hunt choices on one application.

  • 1st choice: Your premium hunt, such as an X zone. This is the only choice that uses your preference points.
  • 2nd and 3rd choices: Hunts you're likely to get, such as the A zone, B zones, or a D zone, so you still have a tag if your first choice doesn't come through.
  • Point only: To build a point without trying for a tag, enter hunt code PD as your first choice. Your purchase must be done by June 2.

Step 4: Understand preference points

  • You earn one deer point each year you don't draw your first-choice premium hunt, even if you draw your second or third choice.
  • You lose all your deer points when you draw your first choice.
  • For premium hunts, 90% of each quota goes to the applicants with the most points. The other 10% is drawn at random among first-choice applicants. Hunts with fewer than 10 tags give one tag by random draw.
  • Apprentice (junior) hunts split 50/50 between points and random draw.
  • The most points anyone can hold for any species is now 24.
  • California has no separate nonresident quota for deer. Residents and nonresidents compete on equal terms.

Some X zones take many years of points. Others draw with only a few. CDFW publishes drawing statistics each year, so check them before you choose.

Step 5: Apply alone or as a party

Party members apply under one Party Identification Number and must list the same hunt choices. The party's point total is the average of its members' points. If a party is larger than the number of tags left in a hunt, it is skipped, not split. If the party isn't drawn, each member earns a point.

Step 6: Check your results

Results are usually posted around mid-June. If you drew a premium tag and later can't hunt, CDFW has a process for returning an unused premium tag to get your points back, but it has strict rules and deadlines, so check the digest before you count on it. Resident deer tag fees are not refundable. Nonresidents who didn't get a tag, or who return an unused non-premium tag before the season opens and before the quota fills, can ask for a refund of the difference between nonresident and resident fees by March 1.

What it costs to apply (2026–27)

License fees include a 3% nonrefundable application fee (up to $7.50 per item), and license agents add a 5% handling fee.

Point rules at a glance

  • System: Preference points for premium deer zones: 90% of tags go to first-choice applicants with the most points and 10% are drawn at random. Unrestricted zones don't need a draw.
  • Nonresident share: None. Residents and nonresidents compete equally for deer tags.
  • You lose your points if: you draw your first-choice premium hunt, or skip the deer drawing for 5 years in a row.
  • Waiting period: None.
  • Parties: Points are averaged without rounding. Every unsuccessful member earns a point.
  • Point only: Put hunt code PD as your first choice on the First Deer Tag Drawing Application.

Full breakdown: how the draw works, with examples · check last year's odds for every hunt

Didn't draw? You still have options

  • Unrestricted tags: A zone, B zone, most D zone, and Archery Only tags are sold until each quota fills. Some fill fast. The B zone tag sold out on August 9 in 2025.
  • Leftover premium tags: Any premium tags left after the drawing go on sale first come, first served on July 2 at 8 a.m.
  • Private land: Ranches in CDFW's Private Lands Management program can issue their own tags, often with longer seasons. Outfitters and hunting leases are a good way in.

Many California outfitters know exactly which zones and hunts they can get you into, and some hold private-land tags that don't depend on the draw. Call them before June 2 if you're booking a guided hunt.

Every Nevada mule deer tag comes from a draw, so the application is the most important part of planning a hunt here. The system rewards patience: your bonus points are squared, so each year you wait counts for more than the last. Here is how it works.

Key dates

These are NDOW's dates for 2026. The 2027 dates will be in next year's regulations, but the calendar has followed a similar pattern for years: guided draw in late winter, main draw in spring.

Step 1: Get hunter education and a license

Anyone born after January 1, 1960, needs proof of hunter education to buy a Nevada hunting license. Nevada accepts hunter education certificates from other states and Canadian provinces if they show your hunter education number and the issuing agency's logo or seal.

You need a current Nevada hunting license to earn bonus points, and it can be bought with your application. You can instead choose to buy the license only if you draw, but that application earns no bonus point.

  • Residents: adult hunting license $38, or combination hunting and fishing $75
  • Nonresidents: adult combination license $155
  • Youth (12–17): $15 combination for residents and nonresidents

Step 2: Choose up to five hunt choices

Each mule deer hunt is a combination of unit group, season, and weapon. You can list up to five choices on one antlered mule deer application, and NDOW recommends using all five. You can submit one antlered mule deer application per draw.

How to think about your five choices:

  • 1st choice: The hunt you really want.
  • 2nd to 5th choices: Hunts with more tags or less demand, so you still hunt if your first choice doesn't come through.
  • Bonus point only: If you want to build points without hunting, you can apply for a bonus point only. You still need a license for that year.

NDOW publishes draw odds and past results each year. Check them before you choose.

Step 3: Understand bonus points

  • Points are squared. Every application gets one draw number. For each bonus point you hold, you get more numbers, equal to your points squared. Four points means 16 extra numbers, or 17 chances in all. Your best (lowest) number is the one that counts.
  • How you earn them: One point each year you apply and don't draw, if you hold a hunting license.
  • Points reset: Your deer points go back to zero when you draw or buy a tag in that category.
  • Don't skip two years: If you fail to apply for two years in a row, you lose your points.
  • Points follow you: If you move to or from Nevada, your points move with you.

Nevada has no guaranteed point-based draw like a preference point system. Even hunters with many points can miss, and a hunter with no points can draw a good tag.

Nonresident quotas: NDOW sets quotas at about 90% for residents and 10% for nonresidents. For many smaller unit groups, that means only one or two nonresident tags.

Step 4: Apply alone or as a party

A party must have at least two hunters, and everyone applies for the same hunts. The party's points are averaged and rounded to the nearest whole number. The group draws together or not at all.

Step 5: Pay the application fees

Application fees are not refundable. You pay the tag fee only if you draw.

A $1 processing fee is also added to license purchases. The $3 game tag application fee lets you choose whether it goes to predator management or to habitat and research for other wildlife.

Point rules at a glance

  • System: Squared bonus points in a fully random draw. Each application gets one number plus extra numbers equal to your points squared, and your lowest number is used. No tags are reserved for top point holders.
  • Nonresident share: About 10% of tags. Nonresidents can also enter a separate guided draw.
  • You lose your points if: you draw or buy an antlered mule deer tag, or don't apply for two years in a row when a season was available.
  • Waiting period: None listed for mule deer in the 2026 regulations.
  • Parties: Points are averaged and rounded to the nearest whole number. The party draws together or not at all.
  • Point only: A $10 Bonus Point Only application during the main draw or the second draw period.

Full breakdown: how the draw works, with examples · check last year's odds for every hunt

Didn't draw? You still have options

  • Second draw (June): A second chance at tags that were not issued in the main draw.
  • First-come, first-served: Tags left after the second draw are sold online on a first-come, first-served basis.
  • Specialty tags: Silver State tags (no bonus points used), Dream tags, and Partnership in Wildlife tags offer a small number of mule deer tags through their own drawings.
  • Hunt another state while you build points. Keep applying every year so you never lose them.

Let an outfitter help

Nevada outfitters can tell you which unit groups they guide and what your odds look like. If you're a nonresident, talk to an outfitter before the guided draw in February.

Montana's nonresident elk draw is really two draws that happen at once. First you apply for a combination license, which gives you a general elk license. At the same time, you can apply for a special elk permit for a limited district. Each one has its own point system. Here is how to put it together.

Key dates (2026)

The 2027 dates have not been posted yet, but the April 1 deadline has been the same for years.

Step 1: Hunter education and prerequisites

If you were born after January 1, 1985, you must show proof of a hunter education course before you apply. You also need a conservation license ($10) and the base hunting license ($50). These are added when you apply and are not refundable.

Step 2: Pick your combination license

There is a 17,000-license quota for the Big Game Combination. You can apply for only one combination license a year. Reduced-price versions exist for youth, college students, Montana natives living out of state, and the Come Home to Hunt program for people with Montana family.

Step 3: Understand preference points

Preference points decide who gets the combination licenses.

  • 75% of nonresident combination licenses go to the applicants with the most preference points.
  • 25% are drawn at random among applicants without preference points. That gives first-time applicants a real chance.
  • A point costs $100. Add it when you apply, or buy one between July 1 and December 31 if you are not applying.
  • Your points are erased when you draw a combination license, or if you skip the next drawing.
  • Outfitter clients can buy a second $100 point when they apply. A license drawn with it is valid only when hunting with a licensed outfitter.

Step 4: Add an elk permit if you want one

Some hunting districts, or certain seasons within them, need a special elk permit on top of your general elk license. The permit is not a second elk; it just lets you use your general license in that district or season.

  • Application fee: $9, nonrefundable.
  • Nonresidents must apply for a combination license at the same time.
  • Bonus points: $20 per permit type when you apply, or $25 if you buy one from July 1 to September 30 without applying.
  • Bonus points are squared. Three points become nine extra entries, plus your application, for ten chances. They count only for your first choice, and they reset when you draw it.

More on the general elk license vs. permits

Step 5: Consider an Elk B license

Elk B licenses are for antlerless elk. They are a second license, so you can take a cow in addition to your general elk. The drawing deadline is June 1 ($275 for nonresidents, including the drawing fee), and some districts sell them over the counter ($270).

What it costs to apply (nonresident example, 2026)

Refunds

If you draw and can't go, you can return a nonresident combination license: 80% back if returned before August 1, and 50% after that until the season starts. Hardship refunds are available for a death or medical emergency (deadline December 1, 2026). Permit fees, the application fee, and prerequisite licenses are not refunded, and your preference points are not restored.

Point rules at a glance

  • Two systems: Nonresident combination licenses (general elk) use preference points: 75% go to the most points and 25% are drawn at random from applicants with zero points. Elk permits and Elk B licenses use squared bonus points (points squared, plus 1, entries) in a random draw.
  • Preference point cap: You can hold at most 3 preference points, so they never stack up past that.
  • Bonus points only count when you buy one: Your bonus points are used only in a year you also buy a bonus point for that drawing.
  • Nonresident share: By law nonresidents are limited to, but not guaranteed, 10% of elk permits.
  • You lose your points if: Bonus points: you draw your first choice in a year you bought a bonus point (skipping years doesn't cost you). Preference points: you draw a combination license, or hold points and skip the next combination drawing.
  • Point only: Bonus point only July 1 – September 30 ($15 resident, $25 nonresident). Nonresident preference point only July 1 – December 31 ($100).

  • Surplus licenses: FWP posts any leftover combination licenses and permits shortly after each drawing.
  • Elk B licenses: Apply by June 1 or buy over the counter where available.
  • Build points: Buy a preference point July 1 – December 31.

Nonresidents get a Montana general deer license through the spring combination license draw. Mule deer permits and antlerless Deer B licenses are separate draws on top of that. Here's how to apply for each.

Key dates (2026)

FWP has not posted 2027 dates yet. The April 1 and June 1 deadlines have been steady for years.

Step 1: Hunter education and prerequisites

Hunters born after January 1, 1985, need proof of hunter education before applying. Every nonresident also needs a $10 conservation license and the $50 base hunting license. Both are nonrefundable.

Step 2: Choose your combination license

You can apply for only one combination license each year. If you only want deer, the Deer Combination is the cheaper choice. If you may want elk too, the Big Game Combination saves a second trip through the draw.

The Landowner-Sponsored option is for hunters who have a landowner (often through an outfitter or a private ranch) willing to sponsor them. It's limited to that landowner's deeded land.

Step 3: Preference points

  • 75% of combination licenses go to applicants with the most preference points.
  • 25% go by random draw to applicants without preference points.
  • Points cost $100 at application, or $100 from July 1 to December 31 if you don't apply.
  • Points are erased when you draw, or if you skip the next drawing.
  • Outfitter clients can buy a second point; licenses drawn with it are valid only when hunting with a licensed outfitter.

Step 4: Deer permits

In some districts, buck mule deer and certain other hunts require a deer permit in addition to your general deer license.

  • Application fee: $5, nonrefundable. Deadline April 1.
  • Nonresidents must apply for a combination license at the same time.
  • A permit is not a second deer. It limits you to the district or portion printed on it.
  • Permits use bonus points: $20 when you apply, or $25 from July 1 to September 30 without applying. Bonus points are squared in the draw and count only for your first choice.

Step 5: Deer B licenses

Deer B licenses are extra antlerless licenses, usually for whitetail does in farm country.

FWP also sells an antlerless whitetail B license valid in one region you choose at purchase. Some B licenses are limited to private land or certain portions of districts.

What it costs to apply (nonresident Deer Combination, 2026)

Refunds

A drawn nonresident combination can be returned for 80% back before August 1 and 50% after that until the season opens. Permit fees, prerequisites, and the application fee are not refunded.

Point rules at a glance

  • Two systems: Nonresident combination licenses (general deer) use preference points: 75% go to the most points and 25% are drawn at random from applicants with zero points. Deer permits and Deer B licenses use squared bonus points (points squared, plus 1, entries) in a random draw.
  • Preference point cap: You can hold at most 3 preference points, so they never stack up past that.
  • Bonus points only count when you buy one: Your bonus points are used only in a year you also buy a bonus point for that drawing.
  • Nonresident share: By law nonresidents are limited to, but not guaranteed, 10% of deer permits.
  • You lose your points if: Bonus points: you draw your first choice in a year you bought a bonus point (skipping years doesn't cost you). Preference points: you draw a combination license, or hold points and skip the next combination drawing.
  • Point only: Bonus point only July 1 – September 30 ($15 resident, $25 nonresident). Nonresident preference point only July 1 – December 31 ($100).

Oregon's controlled hunts are where you'll find most eastern Oregon rifle bull tags, the northeast Oregon archery units, muzzleloader hunts, and antlerless hunts. The system is simple once you know the rules, but one detail matters more than any other: preference points only work on your first choice. Here's how it works.

Key dates

The 2027 dates will be in next year's regulations, but May 15 has been the deadline for years.

Step 1: Buy an annual hunting license

You need a current-year game-hunting license before you can apply. It is added to your application online.

The license and stamps are not refunded if you don't draw. Hunters under 18 need a hunter education number before they can buy a game-hunting license.

Step 3: Choose your hunt codes

Each New Mexico elk hunt has a code that sets the unit, dates, weapon, and bag limit. The middle digit tells you the weapon: 1 is any legal sporting arm, 2 is bow only, and 3 is muzzleloader (or bow or crossbow).

You can list up to three hunt choices. For deer and elk, you can add a fourth choice that is a quadrant of the state. If you draw your fourth choice, you must accept whatever hunt you get in that quadrant, and there are no refunds.

All three choices are considered before the computer moves to the next applicant, so your second and third choices matter. Use them for hunts you would actually be happy to take.

Bag limits for nonresidents: Nonresidents can apply for mature bull (MB) and either-sex (ES) hunts. Antlerless elk licenses and hunts held only on state wildlife management areas are reserved for residents.

Step 4: Understand the pools

New Mexico splits its draw licenses three ways:

To use the outfitter pool, you need a signed contract with a registered outfitter, and you list their registration number on your application. In some units the outfitter pool can give nonresidents better odds than the 6% pool, but it is shared with residents and odds vary by hunt code, so check the department's draw odds. If you draw through it, you hunt with that outfitter, who must guide you for at least two days.

Step 5: Apply alone or as a group

Up to three people can attach to an existing application for most species, for four hunters total. Everyone must be eligible for all of the hunt codes listed. The group draws together or not at all.

This is where New Mexico differs from most states. When you submit your application, your card is charged the full license fee, which includes a nonrefundable application fee. Once an application is paid, you can't edit it. To change anything, you have to delete it and reapply, paying again.

A quality or high-demand elk hunt costs $998 instead of $773. Resident bull and either-sex licenses are $100, and antlerless licenses are $70.

Nonresident elk licenses in Wyoming are issued through a draw, with any leftovers sold afterward. The good news is that the system is fairly simple and a quarter of the licenses go out at random, so even a first-year applicant can draw. The catch is the deadline: nonresident elk applications close in late January or early February (February 2 in 2026), months before most other states. Here is how it works.

Key dates

These are WGFD's dates for the 2026 draw. The 2027 dates have not been posted yet, but the calendar has followed the same pattern for years.

Residents apply January 2 – June 1 and get results June 18.

Step 1: Get your hunter education card

Anyone born on or after January 1, 1966, must have a hunter education certificate to hunt with a firearm in Wyoming. Cards from other states are accepted. Hunter education is required for every hunter in Grand Teton National Park (Area 75), regardless of age.

Step 2: Choose regular or special price

This is the first big decision.

  • Regular price: $707 for a nonresident elk license (includes a fishing license and the $15 application fee).
  • Special price: $1,965. Wyoming sets aside 40% of nonresident elk licenses for applicants willing to pay an extra $1,258. Special applicants compete only against each other, in a separate preference point and random draw.

Because fewer people pay for special price, it often takes fewer points to draw the same hunt. Many hunters use special to draw a hunt years sooner than they could at regular price.

Step 3: Pick region general or limited quota

  • Region general license: You choose one of three nonresident regions (Eastern, Southern, or Western). The license is good in any hunt area in that region that is not fully limited quota.
  • Limited quota license: You choose a specific hunt area and license type, such as Type 1 (any elk), Type 4 or 6 (antlerless or cow/calf), or Type 9 (archery only).

You can list up to three choices. Only your first choice uses your preference points.

Learn more about general and limited quota licenses

Step 4: Understand preference points

  • 75% of licenses in each hunt area and type go to the applicants with the most points.
  • 25% go by random draw. Everyone who misses in the point draw goes into the random draw, whatever their points.
  • Earning points: Nonresidents build elk points by buying a preference point for $52 ($10 for youth) between July 1 and November 2. Missing the draw does not earn you a point by itself.
  • Losing points: Your points go to zero when you draw your first choice in the initial draw. You also lose all of them if you don't buy a preference point for two years in a row. Applying alone doesn't protect them.
  • Reduced price cow/calf licenses do not use points.

Step 5: Apply alone or as a party

Up to six hunters can apply together. Everyone must apply for the same draw (regular or special), hunt area, and license type. The party's points are averaged, and the whole party draws together or not at all. Residents and nonresidents cannot apply together. A party does not improve your odds.

Step 6: Pay and wait

Wyoming charges your card for the full license fee when you apply. If you do not draw, the license fee is refunded to the same card after the draw, but the application fee and any donations are kept. Card payments also carry a 2.5% processing fee.

What it costs to apply (nonresident, 2026)

You will also need a $21.50 conservation stamp once you draw, and an archery license if you hunt the archery season.

Point rules at a glance

  • System: Nonresidents only: 75% of licenses in each hunt area and type go to the most preference points, and 25% are drawn at random among everyone who missed. Regular and special-price applicants draw in separate pools. Residents have no points and draw at random.
  • Nonresident share: Set by hunt area. 40% of nonresident licenses are reserved for special-price applicants.
  • You lose your points if: you draw your first choice in the initial draw, or go two years in a row without buying a preference point.
  • Waiting period: None.
  • Parties: Up to 6, with points averaged. Everyone must apply in the same price pool, and residents and nonresidents can't mix.
  • Point only: Nonresidents buy a point July 1 – November 2. Points are only earned by buying one, and you can't buy one in a year you drew your first choice.

Didn't draw? You still have options

  • Leftover draw (late June): Licenses left after the initial draw. Points are not used.
  • First come, first served (mid-July): Anything left after the leftover draw goes on sale.
  • Cow/calf licenses: You can apply for one reduced price cow/calf license in the initial draw on top of your full price license, and pick up more in the leftover draw or over the counter where available. You can hold up to three elk licenses a year.
  • Build points: Buy a point between July 1 and November 2 to stay in the game for next year.

Utah uses two different point systems for deer. General-season buck permits use preference points, where the most points draw first. Step 1: Get your license

You need a Utah hunting or combination license to apply for a permit or a point. Anyone born after December 31, 1965, must have hunter education.

Nonresidents can apply for all limited-entry and once-in-a-lifetime species plus one general-season species. If you want a general-season deer permit and a general-season elk permit, note that general elk permits are sold over the counter, not drawn.

  • You choose general-season hunts by unit and weapon: archery, muzzleloader, any legal weapon (rifle), and in some units early any legal weapon or restricted weapons.

  • Every time you apply for a general buck deer permit and don't draw, you get a preference point. You lose your points when you draw.
  • Youth get 20% of the general-season buck deer permits.

Draw odds vary widely by unit and weapon. Rifle hunts in popular units often take more points than archery hunts or less popular units. Check past draw results in the Utah Hunt Planner.

  • The other half are drawn at random, with one extra entry for each bonus point.

Premium units, the Henry Mountains and Paunsaugunt, are among the hardest deer permits in the West to draw.

Up to four hunters can apply together for general-season deer and limited-entry deer. Everyone draws together or not at all.

A lot of Alaska hunting doesn't require a draw at all. General season hunts use a free harvest ticket, and registration permits are usually unlimited. But many of the most sought-after hunts, including Kodiak brown bear, some caribou herds, and limited moose hunts, are drawing permits. Here is how Alaska's draw works and how it fits with the other hunt types.

Key dates

ADF&G runs one application period each year. You apply in late fall for hunts that start the following July or later.

For the hunts in the current 2026–2027 regulatory year, applications ran November 1 – December 15, 2025. Applications for 2027–2028 hunts are expected to follow the same window, November 1 – December 15, 2026; confirm in the 2027–2028 supplement.

Step 1: Buy a hunting license

You need a valid Alaska hunting license before you apply. Residents 17 and younger are the exception. ADF&G accepts a license for the current year or for the year the hunt takes place, and you can buy next year's license online.

You don't need to buy a nonresident locking tag to apply. You buy the tag before you go hunting.

Step 2: Read the Drawing Permit Hunt Supplement

Every drawing hunt has a hunt number, like DM for moose, DC for caribou and DB for brown bear. The supplement lists each hunt's area, season, bag limit, how many permits are offered, and who can apply. Many hunts are resident only. Others are nonresident only, or are split between guided and unguided nonresidents.

Read the fine print. Some hunts have antler restrictions, special orientation requirements, or rules that keep you from drawing the same hunt two years in a row.

Step 3: Choose up to six hunts per species

You can submit up to six applications per species. That count includes party applications and any repeat applications for the same hunt. If you go over six for a species, ADF&G rejects all of your applications for that species.

You can apply for the same hunt more than once, which gives you more chances in that one drawing. A few hunts, including Kodiak brown bear and some limited moose hunts, limit guided nonresidents to one application per hunt.

Step 4: Pay the application fees

Fees are not refunded. Applications are online only.

Step 5: Know the nonresident rules

  • Guide-required species. For brown/grizzly bear, Dall sheep and mountain goat, a nonresident must hunt with an Alaska-licensed guide or a qualifying resident relative.
  • Guide-client contract. For guided drawing hunts, you need a signed guide-client agreement before you apply. Your guide's Unique Verification Code (UVC) must be entered on the application. Line up your guide well before December.
  • Hunting with a relative. If a resident relative within the second degree of kindred will accompany you, you choose that option on the application. Some hunts set aside a small number of permits for nonresidents guided by relatives.
  • No guarantee. Drawing a permit doesn't guarantee a guide will be available. Book first, then apply.

Read the full nonresident guide requirement

Step 6: Party applications

Two hunters can apply together on one application, and both get permits if it's drawn. If either one is ineligible, the whole application is thrown out. Two nonresidents hunting with a resident relative can't apply as a party.

There are no points

Alaska does not use preference or bonus points. Every draw is a fresh lottery. That's good news for a first-time applicant, since you have the same odds as someone who has applied for 20 years. It also means you can't build toward a hunt.

Important rules after you draw

  • You can hold only one drawing permit per species per regulatory year.
  • If you don't report on a permit, you can't get permits the next year.
  • Permits can't be transferred.
  • Permit numbers can change after surveys, and hunts can be closed by emergency order.

Registration permits and general hunts: no draw needed

General season hunts only need a free harvest ticket. Many nonresident moose, caribou, sheep and deer hunts are general season hunts.

Registration permits are usually unlimited. You pick them up in person, by mail, or online during a set window before or during the season. Some brown bear hunts, including parts of Southeast Alaska and Unit 23, and some moose hunts in Units 9 and 17 use registration permits. These hunts close early by emergency order if the harvest quota is met.

Draw rules at a glance

  • System: No points. Every drawing hunt is a pure lottery, so your odds don't improve by applying year after year.
  • Limits: One drawing permit per species per regulatory year, and you can't win the same drawing hunt two years in a row (undersubscribed permits excepted).

  • Kodiak brown bear: Fall Kodiak permit winners can't draw a Kodiak permit the next spring. Guided nonresidents get one application per Kodiak hunt, and relative-guided nonresidents are capped at 4 per season.
  • Nonresidents: Shares are set hunt by hunt. Brown bear, Dall sheep and mountain goat require a licensed guide or a resident relative within the second degree of kindred.
  • Parties: A party of two shares one draw number, and the whole application is invalid if either member isn't eligible.

You don't need to draw anything to hunt elk in Washington. General season tags are sold over the counter. Special permits are extra: they let you hunt units, seasons or animals the general season doesn't cover, such as quality bull hunts with few hunters, antlerless hunts, and hunts for youth, seniors and hunters with disabilities. Here's how the drawing works.

Key dates

The 2027 dates will be in next year's pamphlet. The application period has been in late April through May in recent years.

Step 1: Buy your license and choose your tag

This is the step that surprises nonresidents. To apply for a deer or elk special permit, you must first buy a hunting license and select your general season transport tag, including the weapon and area. Only then can you buy a special permit application.

Youth under 16 pay $29.82 for an elk license and $5.05 per application. A 2.9% processing fee is added to card purchases made online or by phone.

Since you're buying the license anyway, you can also hunt the general season with the tag you chose.

Step 2: Pick your permit categories

Washington sorts elk permits into categories. You apply once per category, and you build points separately in each one.

Step 3: Choose your hunts

You can list up to four hunt choices on an application. Quality hunts allow only two. The drawing looks at your choices in order. Hunt numbers, dates and permit counts are in the Big Game pamphlet's elk special permit section.

Step 4: Understand how points work

  • Each application earns you one point in that category.
  • Points can't be moved between categories or people.
  • Washington uses a weighted system. More points improve your odds, but the draw is still random. Hunters with zero points can draw.
  • When you're drawn, your points in that category drop to zero.
  • If you want to build points without hunting, choose the "point saver" option.

Nonresidents apply through the same system. The pamphlet's application instructions don't list a separate nonresident quota, but the nonresident application fee is much higher.

Step 5: Apply alone or in a group

Elk applications can have up to eight hunters in a group (two for multi-season). The leader applies first, and each member applies using the leader's WILD ID. The group's points are averaged, everyone must be eligible for the hunts chosen, and if the group is drawn, everyone gets a permit.

If there are fewer permits for a hunt than people in your group, the group size is capped to the number of permits.

Step 6: Check your results

Results are posted to your WILD account by the end of June and emailed to the address on file. They aren't in the mobile app. It's on you to check.

If you draw a permit you can't use, call WDFW at (360) 902-2515 at least two weeks before the season to return it and get your points back. WDFW has also allowed hunters worried about wildfire to return permits and have points reinstated.

Multi-season elk tags

A multi-season tag lets you hunt elk in the archery, muzzleloader and modern firearm general seasons in units open to those seasons, on both sides of the state. It's awarded by drawing only, through a separate application (for 2026, December 1, 2025 – March 31, 2026, with results in April). If you're drawn, the tag costs $250.97 in 2026, on top of your license.

Point rules at a glance

  • System: Squared points. Your points in a category are squared to set your number of entries in a fully random drawing, so 3 points means 9 entries. Nothing is reserved for top point holders.
  • Points by category: Points are tracked separately for each elk permit category you apply for.
  • Nonresident share: None set. Residents and nonresidents enter the same drawing.
  • You lose your points if: you are drawn in that category (points reset to zero). Current rules describe no expiration for skipped years.
  • Groups: Up to 8 hunters (2 for multi-season), with points averaged.
  • Point only: Choose the Point Saver option on the special permit application. It costs the same as an application.

Didn't draw?

  • Hunt the general season. Your general season tag is still good. See how general season tags work.
  • Raffles and auctions. WDFW runs raffles, and conservation groups auction a few big game permits.
  • Apply again. Your point carries forward.

A general season tag is all you need to hunt deer in Washington. Special permits are a bonus: they open hunts with lower hunter numbers, better bucks, antlerless deer, or dates outside the general seasons. Many hunters apply every year just to build points. Here's how the drawing works.

Key dates

The 2027 dates will be in next year's pamphlet. Recent application windows have run from late April through May.

Step 1: Buy your license and choose your tag

Before you can buy a deer special permit application, you must buy a hunting license and select your general season transport tag, including your hunt method. This means a nonresident pays for the full deer license before applying.

Youth under 16 pay $29.82 for a deer license and $5.05 per application. A 2.9% processing fee is added to card purchases online or by phone.

Step 2: Pick your permit categories

Deer permits are sorted into categories. You apply once per category you qualify for (up to seven deer applications in all) and build points separately in each. The main categories:

There are also categories for youth, hunters 65 and over, hunters with disabilities, Master Hunters, and multi-season tags (a separate application). A Second Deer permit requires a second deer tag using the same weapon as your first tag.

Check the pamphlet's deer special permit section for the full list of hunts, dates and permit numbers. Some private timberland owners limit access or charge fees, so don't apply for a hunt unless you can get access.

Step 3: Choose your hunts

List up to four hunt choices on a regular application, or two on a quality application. The drawing considers them in the order you list them. Each permit you draw needs its own hunting report, on top of your general season report. If you're hunting under a hunter education deferral, you can't apply.

Step 4: Understand how points work

  • Each application earns one point in that category.
  • Points can't be moved between categories or people.
  • The drawing is weighted. More points help, but it's still a lottery, and new applicants can draw.
  • Getting drawn resets your points in that category to zero.
  • The "point saver" option builds a point without entering you in a hunt.

Step 5: Apply alone or in a group

Deer groups can have up to eight hunters (two for multi-season). The leader applies first, members apply with the leader's WILD ID, and points are averaged. If the group draws, everyone gets a permit and can take a deer.

Step 6: Check results

Results are posted in your WILD account by the end of June and emailed to you. If you can't use a permit, call WDFW at (360) 902-2515 at least two weeks before the season to return it and restore your points.

Multi-season deer tags

A multi-season deer tag lets you hunt the archery, muzzleloader and modern firearm general seasons in units open to those seasons. It's awarded by drawing only, through a separate application (for 2026, December 1, 2025 – March 31, 2026, with results in April). If drawn, the tag costs $191.77 in 2026.

Other limited-entry options

  • Scotch Creek. WDFW runs a limited-access deer hunt at the Scotch Creek Wildlife Area.
  • Raffles and auctions. WDFW raffles a few deer permits, and conservation groups auction others.
  • Second deer tags. Residents pay $68.48 and nonresidents $356.90 for a second deer tag where one is allowed.

Point rules at a glance

  • System: Squared points. Your points in a category are squared to set your number of entries in a fully random drawing, so 3 points means 9 entries. Nothing is reserved for top point holders.
  • Points by category: Points are tracked separately for each deer permit category you apply for.
  • Nonresident share: None set. Residents and nonresidents enter the same drawing.
  • You lose your points if: you are drawn in that category (points reset to zero). Current rules describe no expiration for skipped years.
  • Groups: Up to 8 hunters (2 for multi-season), with points averaged.
  • Point only: Choose the Point Saver option on the special permit application. It costs the same as an application.
